questions.stem: A 34 year old woman who moved to the UK from a remote mountain village in Nepal 2 months ago has a 1 year history of tiredness, cold intolerance and weight gain. She has a large, smooth, non-tender goitre. She takes no medications and has never had neck surgery. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm. TSH is raised and free T4 is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypothyroidism?
questions.e: Worldwide, iodine deficiency is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism and goitre (Nepal, Africa, Asia, South America); Hashimoto's leads in developed countries.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: TSH is raised and free T4 is low
steps.x: Primary hypothyroidism with a goitre in someone from an iodine-deficient region.

elim: Painful, tender goitre with a thyrotoxic phase after a viral illness; hers is painless.
Causes thyrotoxicosis (low TSH, high T4), the opposite of her results.
The commonest cause in developed countries, but her origin points to the commonest cause worldwide.
Nodular, over 50s, and causes hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism.

steps.x: **D. Iodine deficiency.** Worldwide = iodine deficiency; UK = Hashimoto's.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman had radioactive iodine for Graves' disease 5 months ago. Her palpitations and weight loss have resolved, but for 6 weeks she has felt tired and cold and has gained 4 kg. Her skin is dry. Her pulse rate is 56 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Radioiodine destroys thyroid tissue and commonly leaves the patient hypothyroid months later; raised TSH with low T4 confirms it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: radioactive iodine for Graves' disease 5 months ago
tired and cold and has gained 4 kg
steps.x: New hypothyroid symptoms months after thyroid ablation.

elim: A carbimazole side effect presenting with sore throat and fever, not weight gain.
A transient thyrotoxic phase of Hashimoto's; she had Graves' treated with radioiodine.
Would cause low TSH and high T4 again, not raised TSH.
Affects the orbits; it does not cause tiredness, weight gain and raised TSH.

steps.x: **C. Hypothyroidism after radioactive iodine.** Radioiodine and thyroid surgery are classic iatrogenic causes.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 6 years. Over 4 months he has become slow, tired and constipated and has gained 6 kg. His mood is stable and he has no thirst or polyuria. His pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 132/86 mmHg. His lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L (0.4–1.0). Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lithium (like amiodarone) is a recognised drug cause of primary hypothyroidism: raised TSH, low free T4.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hypothyroid features in a patient on a drug known to block thyroid hormone release.

elim: Low mood can cause slowing, but not bradycardia, raised TSH and low T4; his mood is stable.
His level is in range, and toxicity gives tremor, ataxia and confusion.
A lithium side effect causing polyuria and thirst, which he denies.
Pituitary failure gives a low or normal TSH, not a raised one.

steps.x: **C. Lithium-induced hypothyroidism.** Lithium and amiodarone: check TFTs.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a 6 month history of tiredness, dry skin, weight gain and heavier periods. She feels the cold more than her colleagues. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 138/88 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows
questions.e: Hertoghe's (Queen Anne's) sign, loss of the outer third of the eyebrows, is a classic sign of hypothyroidism.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: tiredness, dry skin, weight gain and heavier periods
steps.x: Classic hypothyroid symptoms with raised TSH and low T4.

elim: Hyperreflexia is a thyrotoxic sign; hypothyroidism slows reflex relaxation.
A sign of thyrotoxicosis and sympathetic overactivity.
Seen in thyrotoxicosis and thyroid eye disease.
Specific to Graves' disease despite its name.

steps.x: **D. Loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows.** Hertoghe sign = hypothyroidism; tremor, lid lag, brisk reflexes = thyrotoxicosis.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl is brought to her GP because her school marks have fallen and she is always tired. She has gained weight and has not grown in height over the last year. She has a firm, painless, diffuse goitre. Her pulse rate is 62 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hashimoto's is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in children in developed countries; TPO antibodies are positive in about 90%.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hypothyroid child with goitre and positive TPO antibodies.

elim: Causes thyrotoxicosis with low TSH; also TPO is not its defining antibody.
Rare in the UK; positive TPO antibodies point to autoimmunity.
Euthyroid enlargement; it does not cause raised TSH or antibodies.
A rapidly enlarging goitre in older adults, usually on a Hashimoto's background.

steps.x: **B. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Autoimmune Hashimoto's is the commonest cause in UK children and adults.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman is found on her kitchen floor in December, drowsy and confused, and has a seizure in the ambulance. She has never been diagnosed with a thyroid problem. Her temperature is 32.4°C, pulse rate 42 bpm and BP 84/52 mmHg. She has periorbital oedema, sparse hair and absent reflexes. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Myxoedema coma is the extreme of hypothyroidism: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hyporeflexia, reduced consciousness and seizures; it can be the first presentation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: periorbital oedema, sparse hair and absent reflexes
steps.x: Hypothermia, bradycardia and coma with myxoedematous features and a very high TSH.

elim: Causes hypotension and hyponatraemia but not hypothermia with raised TSH and very low T4.
Her glucose is normal.
Would not explain hypothermia, bradycardia and the thyroid results.
Possible precipitant, but sepsis alone does not give TSH 72 and undetectable T4.

steps.x: **D. Myxoedema coma.** Confusion + hypothermia + bradycardia + high TSH = myxoedema coma.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with hypothyroidism has taken levothyroxine reliably for 10 years. He was admitted 3 days ago with a productive cough and right basal crackles. Today he is drowsy and confused. His temperature is 33.8°C, pulse rate 46 bpm and BP 88/56 mmHg. TSH is 48 mU/L and free T4 is 4 pmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely precipitant of his deterioration?
questions.e: Myxoedema coma is usually triggered by infection, cold exposure or stopping thyroid replacement; his pneumonia is the trigger.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: productive cough and right basal crackles
steps.x: Decompensated hypothyroidism appearing during a pneumonia.

elim: Iodine excess is not a recognised precipitant here; he has no exposure.
Fluids treat hypotension; they do not precipitate myxoedema coma.
A common trigger, but he takes it reliably.
Not a recognised precipitant.

steps.x: **A. Chest infection.** Triggers: infection, cold, stopping levothyroxine.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman is admitted with myxoedema coma. Her temperature is 32.9°C, pulse rate 44 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 8 breaths per minute. She is increasingly drowsy and her ankles and lung bases are becoming oedematous. Arterial blood gas shows a raised PaCO2.
questions.q: Which is the most serious complication she is developing?
questions.e: Untreated myxoedema coma progresses to heart failure and respiratory failure; slow breathing with a rising PaCO2 shows hypoventilation.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hypoventilation with CO2 retention in a hypometabolic patient.

elim: A complication of thyrotoxicosis; she is bradycardic.
Not a feature of myxoedema coma.
Causes hypoxia with a low PaCO2 and tachycardia, not slow breathing.
The thyrotoxic emergency, the opposite state.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory failure.** Myxoedema coma can progress to heart and respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with type 1 diabetes and coeliac disease has 4 months of tiredness, constipation and 5 kg weight gain. Her insulin needs have fallen slightly. She has no abdominal pain or diarrhoea and follows a gluten-free diet. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. She has a small diffuse goitre.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hashimoto's shares HLA-DR3/DR5 susceptibility with type 1 diabetes and coeliac disease, so autoimmune clusters are common.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hypothyroid features and goitre in someone with other autoimmune diseases.

elim: Also autoimmune, but causes weight loss, pigmentation and hypotension.
Would cause diarrhoea and weight loss; she is adherent to the diet.
Causes vomiting and early satiety, not a goitre and weight gain.
Causes tiredness and glossitis but not goitre, constipation and weight gain.

steps.x: **D. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Autoimmune diseases cluster: think Hashimoto's in T1DM and coeliac disease.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman had 6 weeks of palpitations, sweating and weight loss 5 months ago, which settled without treatment. She now has tiredness, cold intolerance and weight gain. She has a firm, non-tender, diffuse goitre. She has not been pregnant recently. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hashimoto's can begin with a transient thyrotoxic 'hashitoxicosis' phase before follicular destruction leaves the patient hypothyroid; TPO antibodies support it.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Brief thyrotoxic phase, then hypothyroid, with a painless goitre and antibodies.

elim: Also has a thyrotoxic then hypothyroid course, but the goitre is painful and tender after a viral illness.
Would not settle and swing into hypothyroidism untreated; TSH receptor antibodies define it.
Follows pregnancy, which she has not had.
A single hot nodule causing persistent hyperthyroidism.

steps.x: **C. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.** Hashitoxicosis: transient hyperthyroid phase, then hypothyroid.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has 3 months of tiredness, constipation and feeling cold. He takes no medications. His pulse rate is 46 bpm and regular, and BP 136/88 mmHg. He has dry skin. ECG (see item resources). Potassium is 4.3 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). TSH is 34 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 5 pmol/L (9–25).

visual.title: Rhythm strip
visual.caption: Sinus bradycardia at 46 bpm with normal PR interval.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his bradycardia?
questions.e: Low thyroid hormone slows heart rate and contractility, giving a sinus bradycardia; the thyroid results explain everything.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: pulse rate is 46 bpm and regular
steps.x: Sinus bradycardia with hypothyroid symptoms and results.

elim: The ECG shows sinus rhythm with every P wave conducted.
He takes no medications.
His potassium is normal.
Possible in older people, but does not explain raised TSH, low T4 and the systemic symptoms.

steps.x: **D. Hypothyroidism.** Sinus bradycardia + raised TSH = hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has 5 months of very heavy periods with clots, tiredness and low mood. She has gained 6 kg and her hair is thinning. Pelvic examination and ultrasound are normal. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her heavy periods?
questions.e: Menorrhagia is a recognised feature of hypothyroidism, along with weight gain, hair thinning and low mood; raised TSH and low T4 confirm primary hypothyroidism.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: Pelvic examination and ultrasound are normal
steps.x: Heavy periods with systemic hypothyroid features and a normal pelvis.

elim: Unlikely at 38 with a normal ultrasound, and does not explain the thyroid results.
Causes infrequent periods, hirsutism and acne rather than menorrhagia.
Pelvic examination and ultrasound are normal.
Lifelong bleeding tendency; does not explain weight gain and hair thinning.

steps.x: **B. Hypothyroidism.** Check TFTs in menorrhagia with hypothyroid features.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has noticed her voice becoming deep and hoarse over 6 months. She also feels slow, cold and tired. She has never smoked and has no difficulty swallowing. Her face looks puffy, particularly around the eyes. Her pulse rate is 56 bpm. Her neck is smooth with no nodules. TSH is 22 mU/L (0.4–4.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hoarse voice?
questions.e: Hoarseness and periorbital puffiness come from myxoedematous tissue deposition in hypothyroidism.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Hoarse voice with periorbital puffiness and slowing.

elim: Hoarseness for 6 months needs thought, but she is a never-smoker and the systemic features and TSH explain it.
Follows neck surgery or malignancy; she has neither.
Does not cause facial puffiness, bradycardia and raised TSH.
Seen in voice overuse and do not explain systemic slowing.

steps.x: **A. Hypothyroidism.** Hoarse voice + periorbital puffiness + raised TSH = hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has had primary hypothyroidism for 8 years. His levothyroxine dose has been unchanged at 125 micrograms daily and his TFTs were normal last year. He now feels tired again. He has not started any new medicines. He admits his routine has been disrupted since starting night shifts. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these results?
questions.e: In a stable, previously diagnosed patient, a raised TSH with low-normal free T4 most often reflects missed doses.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.

clues: routine has been disrupted since starting night shifts
steps.x: Established patient, unchanged dose, new rise in TSH with low-normal T4.

elim: Would present with a rapidly enlarging neck mass.
Pituitary failure gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH, not a raised one.
Would show a low TSH.
Gives high TSH with a high free T4, not low-normal.

steps.x: **D. Suboptimal adherence to levothyroxine.** Ask about adherence before increasing the dose.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has a TSH of 7.1 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 14 pmol/L (9–25) on two tests 3 months apart. She has no symptoms and is not planning a pregnancy. She is keen to know whether she is likely to develop an underactive thyroid in future.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess her risk of progression?
questions.e: In subclinical hypothyroidism, positive TPO antibodies suggest Hashimoto's and a higher risk of progression to overt disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.

clues: likely to develop an underactive thyroid in future
steps.x: Subclinical hypothyroidism: raised TSH, normal T4, no symptoms.

elim: Used to find the cause of thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroid risk.
A tumour marker after thyroid cancer treatment.
Assesses nodules, not autoimmune progression risk.
Support Graves' disease, a cause of thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **C. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies.** TPO antibodies predict progression in subclinical disease.

questions.stem: A 53 year old man has routine bloods at a health check. He feels well with no symptoms. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Examination is normal. TSH is 6.4 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 15 pmol/L (9–25). Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat thyroid function tests in 1 week
Repeat thyroid function tests in 3–6 months
questions.e: A raised TSH with normal T4 and no symptoms is subclinical hypothyroidism; repeat TFTs in 3–6 months to see whether it persists.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Subclinical hypothyroidism found incidentally.

elim: Too soon; TSH changes over weeks to months.
Not indicated for a single mildly raised TSH without symptoms.
There is no goitre or nodule to assess.
Used in thyrotoxicosis, not raised TSH.

steps.x: **B. Repeat thyroid function tests in 3–6 months.** Subclinical: confirm on repeat in 3–6 months before deciding.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has noticed a swelling in her neck over 3 months. She also has tiredness, constipation and dry skin. She has no neck pain. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 130/84 mmHg. She has a smooth, diffuse, non-tender goitre that moves on swallowing, with no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Thyroid function tests are the gold standard and first test for suspected hypothyroidism; everything else follows the result.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Diffuse goitre with hypothyroid symptoms: first confirm thyroid status.

elim: Used for a suspicious discrete nodule, not a smooth diffuse goitre.
Used to find the cause of thyrotoxicosis once TFTs show it.
Help find the cause once hypothyroidism is confirmed on TFTs.
Not the first test for a diffuse goitre with hypothyroid symptoms.

steps.x: **C. Thyroid function tests.** TFTs first, always.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has 6 months of weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and low mood. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 140/90 mmHg. Her ankle reflexes relax slowly. She has had no neck surgery or radioiodine and takes no medications. Thyroid function tests are requested.
questions.q: Which result is most likely?
questions.e: In primary hypothyroidism the failing thyroid makes little T4, and loss of negative feedback drives a high TSH.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Clinical primary hypothyroidism.

elim: Seen with a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, not her picture.
Thyrotoxicosis.
Secondary (pituitary) hypothyroidism, which is much rarer.
Euthyroid; would not explain her signs.

steps.x: **B. TSH high, free T4 low.** Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH, low free T4.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman started levothyroxine 50 micrograms daily 10 days ago for primary hypothyroidism. She returns saying she still feels tired and asks whether the dose should be increased. She is taking the tablets every morning. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Check TFTs today and adjust the dose
Continue the current dose and recheck TFTs at 6 weeks
Stop levothyroxine and recheck in 3 months
questions.e: TSH has a half-life of about 4–6 weeks, so TFTs are checked 4–6 weeks after starting or changing levothyroxine.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Too early after starting treatment to judge the dose.

elim: Not used routinely, and it is far too early to judge response.
TSH takes 4–6 weeks to reach a new steady state, so a result now is misleading.
Too early; she has not reached steady state.
She has overt hypothyroidism and needs treatment.

steps.x: **C. Continue the current dose and recheck TFTs at 6 weeks.** Recheck TFTs 4–6 weeks after any dose change.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has a 4 month history of tiredness, weight gain and constipation. She has a firm, rubbery, painless diffuse goitre. Her mother has vitiligo. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm. TSH is 18 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 7 pmol/L (9–25). An antibody test is sent to confirm the cause.
questions.q: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
questions.e: Anti-TPO antibodies are found in about 90% of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and drive lymphocytic destruction of the gland.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what test answers the clinical question being asked.
Hypothyroidism with a painless goitre and an autoimmune family history.

elim: Pernicious anaemia, a separate autoimmune disease.
Coeliac disease.
Non-specific; used in SLE and connective tissue disease.
Graves' disease, which causes thyrotoxicosis.

steps.x: **B. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies.** Hashimoto's = anti-TPO positive in 90%.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has had hypothyroidism for 5 years; her TFTs are normal on levothyroxine 100 micrograms. She has 3 months of increasing tiredness and breathlessness on stairs. Her periods are heavy. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm. She has pale conjunctivae. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Tiredness and breathlessness with a low MCV in a treated hypothyroid patient should raise suspicion of co-existing iron deficiency anaemia; confirm with ferritin.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Normal TFTs but new symptoms with a microcytic anaemia.

elim: Her TFTs are normal; extra thyroid hormone will not correct the anaemia.
Her TSH is in range, so her dose is correct.
She is symptomatic with a microcytic anaemia that needs investigating.
The low MCV points to iron deficiency rather than heart failure.

steps.x: **B. Check serum ferritin.** Treated hypothyroid + low MCV: look for iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman takes levothyroxine 150 micrograms daily for Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Her dose was increased 2 months ago. She now has palpitations, feels hot and has lost 2 kg. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and regular. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: A low TSH on levothyroxine means over-replacement: reduce the dose (TSH low → reduce; TSH high → increase).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: Her dose was increased 2 months ago
steps.x: Over-replacement symptoms after a dose increase with suppressed TSH.

elim: Antithyroid drugs are wrong; she is simply over-replaced.
Her TSH is suppressed; more would worsen it.
This is iatrogenic over-replacement, not Graves' disease.
She still needs replacement, at a lower dose.

steps.x: **C. Reduce the levothyroxine dose.** TSH low on levothyroxine → reduce the dose.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 4 month history of tiredness, weight gain and cold intolerance. Her pulse rate is 60 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. She has no cardiac history and is not pregnant. TSH is 32 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 6 pmol/L (9–25). Anti-TPO antibodies are positive.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) is first-line replacement, with TSH monitored and the dose adjusted gradually.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Overt primary hypothyroidism from Hashimoto's.

elim: An antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism; it would worsen her condition.
Synthetic T3 is not first-line replacement.
An antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism.
She has overt symptomatic hypothyroidism and needs replacement.

steps.x: **B. Levothyroxine.** Levothyroxine is first-line.

questions.stem: A 77 year old man with stable angina and a previous coronary stent is diagnosed with primary hypothyroidism (TSH 26 mU/L, free T4 6 pmol/L). His GP plans to start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms daily and increase slowly rather than starting at a full replacement dose.
questions.q: Which adverse effect is this cautious approach mainly intended to avoid?
questions.e: In the elderly and those with ischaemic heart disease, high starting doses increase myocardial oxygen demand and can precipitate angina, arrhythmia and cardiac stress.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: stable angina and a previous coronary stent
steps.x: Elderly man with IHD starting thyroid replacement.

elim: A side effect of carbimazole, not levothyroxine.
Not a dose-related effect of levothyroxine.
Caused by untreated disease, not treatment.
Not related to levothyroxine dosing.

steps.x: **E. Worsening angina.** Start low, go slow in IHD: avoids angina and arrhythmia.

questions.stem: A 63 year old postmenopausal woman has taken levothyroxine for 15 years. Her TSH has been at the lower end of normal for some time. She asks her GP whether there are any long-term risks from her tablets. She has no cardiac history.
questions.q: Which long-term risk is most associated with her treatment?
questions.e: Levothyroxine increases bone turnover, raising the risk of osteoporosis and fracture in postmenopausal women, especially if over-replaced.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Long-term thyroid replacement in a postmenopausal woman.

elim: Linked to carbimazole and propylthiouracil.
Not caused by levothyroxine.
Not a recognised effect of levothyroxine.
Hypothyroidism, not its treatment, causes weight gain.

steps.x: **B. Fragility fracture.** Levothyroxine: watch bone health after the menopause.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has been stable on levothyroxine 100 micrograms for 4 years. Three months ago she was started on calcium carbonate with vitamin D after a wrist fracture, and she takes all her tablets together with breakfast. Her TSH has risen from 1.9 to 8.2 mU/L (0.4–4.0). She says she never misses doses.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Take levothyroxine 4 hours apart from the calcium
Take levothyroxine with the calcium at night
questions.e: Calcium carbonate, iron, digoxin and HRT reduce levothyroxine absorption; space them by about 4 hours.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
TSH rose after starting calcium taken at the same time.

elim: Treats the number, not the cause; the interaction would persist.
She needs bone protection after a fragility fracture.
Not indicated; absorption is the problem.
Taking them together is what reduces absorption.

steps.x: **D. Take levothyroxine 4 hours apart from the calcium.** Separate levothyroxine from calcium and iron.

questions.stem: An 86 year old man has a TSH of 7.8 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 of 13 pmol/L (9–25), confirmed on repeat 3 months later. He has mild memory problems that have been stable for years. He has no new tiredness, weight gain or constipation. His pulse rate is 70 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: In people over 80 with TSH 5.5–10 mU/L, a watch-and-wait approach is recommended (NICE NG145).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.
Very elderly with mild subclinical hypothyroidism.

elim: In the over 80s with TSH 5.5–10, treatment gives no benefit and risks over-replacement.
Too high for an elderly man and not indicated.
Never used for subclinical disease.
Does not change management of a mildly raised TSH.

steps.x: **E. Watch and wait.** Over 80 with TSH 5.5–10: watch and wait.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness and low mood. TSH was 8.1 mU/L and then 7.6 mU/L (0.4–4.0) 3 months apart, with free T4 of 13 and 12 pmol/L (9–25). She is not planning pregnancy. Examination is normal. Other causes of tiredness have been excluded.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Under 65 with TSH 5.5–10 on two occasions 3 months apart and hypothyroid symptoms: consider a 6-month trial of levothyroxine.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: 6 months of tiredness and low mood
steps.x: Symptomatic subclinical hypothyroidism under 65, confirmed twice.

elim: For hyperthyroidism.
She is symptomatic with a persistently raised TSH, so a trial is reasonable.
Ignores her persistent symptoms.
Not used in hypothyroidism.

steps.x: **D. Six-month trial of levothyroxine.** Under 65, symptomatic, TSH 5.5–10 twice: 6-month levothyroxine trial.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman is admitted to intensive care with myxoedema coma. Her temperature is 32.6°C, pulse rate 40 bpm and BP 80/48 mmHg. Sodium is 124 mmol/L (135–145). The endocrine team advise giving IV hydrocortisone before or alongside IV levothyroxine until a random cortisol result is available.
questions.q: Which is the main reason for giving hydrocortisone?
questions.e: Thyroid hormone raises metabolic demand for cortisol; with possible adrenal insufficiency, giving levothyroxine alone could precipitate adrenal crisis. Hydrocortisone continues until adrenal insufficiency is excluded.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: until a random cortisol result is available
steps.x: Steroid cover is given until the adrenal axis is known.

elim: Thyroid storm is a thyrotoxic emergency; it is not the concern here.
Not the reason for steroid cover in myxoedema coma.
TSH falls once thyroid hormone is replaced; this is not the aim.
Glucose would be given for hypoglycaemia; steroids are for adrenal cover.

steps.x: **A. Possible co-existing adrenal insufficiency.** Myxoedema coma: IV hydrocortisone until adrenal insufficiency excluded.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with untreated hypothyroidism is brought in drowsy after a week of cold weather. His temperature is 33.1°C, pulse rate 44 bpm, BP 86/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute. He has periorbital oedema and slow-relaxing reflexes. TSH is 61 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is <3 pmol/L (9–25).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Active rewarming and discharge when warm
questions.e: Myxoedema coma is managed in ICU with IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine, supportive care and senior endocrine input.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs now, at this point in the pathway.

clues: drowsy after a week of cold weather
steps.x: Myxoedema coma: an emergency needing IV hormone and steroid cover.

elim: Treats only the hypothermia, not the life-threatening hormone deficiency.
Carbimazole is oral and treats hyperthyroidism.
Thyroid hormone without steroid cover risks adrenal crisis.
Too slow and poorly absorbed in a comatose patient.

steps.x: **C. IV hydrocortisone and IV levothyroxine.** IV hydrocortisone + IV levothyroxine in ICU, with endocrine input.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has 6 months of tiredness and weight gain. TSH is 28 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 6 pmol/L (9–25). Anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Her pituitary function is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Where is the primary abnormality causing these results?
questions.e: Primary hypothyroidism: the thyroid fails, T4 falls and loss of negative feedback causes a compensatory rise in TSH.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
High TSH with low T4: the pituitary is responding normally.

elim: Pituitary failure would give a low or normal TSH.
Hypothalamic failure would also give a low TSH.
Hormone resistance is rare and would give a high T4.
Secretes ADH and oxytocin, not TSH.

steps.x: **E. Thyroid gland.** High TSH + low T4 = gland failure (primary).

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 4 months of hard stools every 4 days, tiredness and weight gain. He takes no opioids or anticholinergic drugs. Rectal examination and colonoscopy are normal. Calcium is 2.36 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). TSH is 21 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 7 pmol/L (9–25).
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his constipation?
questions.e: Low thyroid hormone slows gut motility, causing constipation, as part of a generally reduced metabolic rate.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: takes no opioids or anticholinergic drugs
steps.x: Constipation in hypothyroidism with other causes excluded.

elim: Colonoscopy is normal.
His calcium is normal.
He takes no constipating drugs.
Does not explain weight gain and abnormal TFTs.

steps.x: **E. Reduced gut motility.** Hypothyroidism slows the gut.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman wears a thick jumper in a warm office. She has gained 7 kg over 6 months despite eating less and feels tired all the time. Her temperature is 36.0°C and pulse rate 56 bpm. Her hands are cool and dry. TSH is 25 mU/L (0.4–4.0) and free T4 is 6 pmol/L (9–25).
questions.q: Which best explains her cold intolerance and weight gain?
questions.e: Insufficient T3/T4 slows basal metabolic rate in almost all tissues, reducing heat production and energy use.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: thick jumper in a warm office
steps.x: Low thyroid hormone, low heat production.

elim: Seen in thyrotoxicosis, giving heat intolerance and weight loss.
Does not explain cold intolerance and the TFTs.
Can cause tiredness but not weight gain with a raised TSH.
Episodic digital colour change, not generalised cold intolerance.

steps.x: **E. Reduced basal metabolic rate.** Hypothyroidism = slowed metabolism everywhere.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Her brother has type 1 diabetes and her mother has Addison's disease. She has a firm, painless goitre and her TSH is 14 mU/L (0.4–4.0). She asks why these autoimmune conditions seem to run together in her family.
questions.q: Which shared genetic factor best explains this clustering?
questions.e: Hashimoto's shares HLA-DR3/DR5 susceptibility with type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, Graves' and Addison's.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Familial clustering of organ-specific autoimmune disease.

elim: Linked to breast and ovarian cancer, not autoimmunity.
Causes haemochromatosis.
Linked to ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.
Linked to Behçet's disease.

steps.x: **E. HLA-DR3.** Organ-specific autoimmunity clusters on HLA-DR3/DR5.
